name: Egyptian
other_names: Ancient Egypt; Pharaonic Egypt; Kemet (self-name, 'the black land')
date_note: c. 3100 BCE (unification) to 30 BCE (Roman annexation); Predynastic before and Roman/Coptic continuities after
making_significance: A state-organised craft system in stone, faience, linen, papyrus and metal whose workshops, tools and named workers are unusually well documented.
materials_techniques: stone carving; faience; linen weaving; papyrus making; copper-bronze casting; gilding; mud brick
object_types: statues; stelae; coffins; faience vessels; jewellery; papyri; linen; furniture
functions: ritual and belief;rule and display;record and writing;clothing and adornment;shelter
defined_by: Greek and Roman writers; Egyptology from Champollion (1822) on; museums; national heritage bodies
leaves_out: Nubian neighbours (and the Kushite 25th Dynasty, often cast as 'foreign'); Libyan/Amazigh and Levantine residents and captives; forced and conscripted labour; the non-elite village makers (e.g. Deir el-Medina workers named individually); Predynastic, Coptic and Islamic Egypt; present-day Egyptians, whose connection is often cut by 'Egyptomania' framing
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Walters Art Museum (CC0);British Museum collection online (link out);Wikimedia Commons;PeriodO
notes: Existing in project. Much museum material is from burials: default-exclude human remains and flag funerary objects.

name: Nubian / Kushite
other_names: Kush; Kerma, Napatan and Meroitic Kush; Ta-Seti
date_note: c. 2500 BCE (Kerma) to c. 350 CE (end of Meroë); Christian Nubian kingdoms follow
making_significance: Nubian workshops produced Kerma polished pottery, Meroitic painted ceramics, gold work and a pyramid-building tradition distinct from Egypt's.
materials_techniques: black-topped and polished pottery; goldsmithing; iron smelting (Meroë); sandstone carving; faience
object_types: pottery; jewellery; pyramids; offering tables; inscriptions in Meroitic script
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;clothing and adornment;exchange and value;record and writing
defined_by: Egyptian texts (as 'Kush'); George Reisner and 20th-century Egyptology; Sudanese archaeology; museums
leaves_out: Treated as Egypt's periphery rather than a centre; C-Group, Pan-Grave and Medjay pastoralists; Christian Nubian kingdoms (Nobadia, Makuria, Alwa); present-day Nubians displaced by the Aswan High Dam (1960s); Meroitic as a still largely untranslated language
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);British Museum collection online (link out);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;PeriodO
notes: Members: ARC Kerma, A-Group, C-Group, Pan-Grave, X-Group. Boston MFA holds Reisner material but images are not open.

name: Aksumite
date_note: c. 1st–10th century CE; conversion to Christianity 4th century
making_significance: Aksum minted gold, silver and bronze coins, raised monolithic stelae and wrote in Ge'ez, trading across the Red Sea.
materials_techniques: monolith quarrying and carving; coin minting; stone architecture; ivory
object_types: stelae; coins; inscriptions; pottery; church architecture
functions: rule and display;exchange and value;record and writing;ritual and belief
defined_by: Greek and Roman sources (Periplus); European travellers; Ethiopian national history; UNESCO (Aksum, 1980)
leaves_out: The pre-Aksumite D'mt period and South Arabian links; pastoralists and the Beja; enslaved people traded across the Red Sea; Ethiopian Orthodox communities for whom the sites remain sacred; later Zagwe and Solomonic periods
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out);open-access excavation reports
notes: Stelae at Aksum are living sacred landscape; the Aksum obelisk was taken to Rome 1937 and returned 2005 (restitution case).

name: Swahili
date_note: c. 8th century CE to present; stone towns flourish c. 1000–1500
making_significance: Coral-stone towns, carved doors, textiles and imported ceramics show African coastal makers working within Indian Ocean trade.
materials_techniques: coral-stone and lime building; wood carving; weaving; bead-making; iron working
object_types: carved doors; mosques and tombs; pillar tombs; textiles; coins; beads
functions: shelter;exchange and value;ritual and belief;rule and display;transport
defined_by: Colonial historiography (often as 'Arab' or 'Persian' colonies); later African archaeology (Chittick, Horton, Chami); Swahili communities
leaves_out: The inland peoples who supplied ivory, gold and grain; enslaved people traded through the coast; the colonial framing that denied African authorship; present-day Swahili-speaking communities of Kenya, Tanzania, Mozambique and Comoros
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;British Museum collection online (link out);open-access excavation reports;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)
notes: Existing in project. Slave trade must be shown as people with content note.

name: Great Zimbabwe
date_note: c. 1100–1450 CE at the main site; wider Zimbabwe tradition c. 1200–1800
making_significance: Dry-stone walling without mortar, soapstone carving and gold trade connected southern African makers to the Indian Ocean.
materials_techniques: dry-stone walling; soapstone carving; gold working; iron smelting; cattle husbandry
object_types: enclosure walls; soapstone birds; gold beads; imported glass and ceramics
functions: rule and display;shelter;exchange and value;ritual and belief
defined_by: Shona oral tradition; colonial writers who denied African authorship (Rhodesian 'Phoenician/Sheba' myth); Gertrude Caton-Thompson (1929) and later African archaeology; UNESCO (1986)
leaves_out: The broader Zimbabwe tradition sites (Khami, Danangombe, Naletale); the Mapungubwe predecessors; farming commoners outside the enclosures; the Shona descendant communities; the colonial denial itself
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out);open-access excavation reports
notes: Soapstone birds were removed in the 1890s; most returned from South Africa (1981, 2003). Check which remain abroad.

name: Nok
date_note: c. 1500 BCE–1 CE for settlement; terracottas from c. 900 BCE
making_significance: Nok communities made some of the earliest large fired-clay sculpture in sub-Saharan Africa and smelted iron.
materials_techniques: terracotta modelling and firing; iron smelting; grinding stones
functions: ritual and belief;tools;food and storage
defined_by: Bernard Fagg (1940s); popular media and the art market ('Nok civilisation')
leaves_out: The name implies a state: evidence shows dispersed farming communities, not a kingdom; neighbouring contemporaries; the looting that destroyed contexts; present-day communities of central Nigeria
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: FLAG: 'civilisation' is misleading; routes to ARC Nok (existing). Terracottas heavily looted and faked; avoid market-sourced images.

name: Ghana / Wagadu
date_note: c. 4th? to 13th century CE; known from Arabic writers from the 8th century
making_significance: Wagadu controlled gold and salt routes across the Sahara, linking Sahelian smiths and weavers to North African markets.
materials_techniques: gold trade; iron working; weaving; mud-brick architecture
object_types: gold; beads; pottery; architecture at Koumbi Saleh
functions: exchange and value;rule and display;transport
defined_by: Arabic geographers (al-Bakri, 1068); Soninke oral tradition; French colonial scholarship
leaves_out: Unrelated to the territory of present-day Ghana; the Soninke name Wagadu; enslaved people traded across the Sahara; Sahelian peoples outside the court; debated identification of Koumbi Saleh as capital
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: Start date poorly known; verify range. Few free object images.

name: Mali
date_note: c. 1235 (Sunjata) to decline c. 1600
making_significance: Mali's courts and cities supported earthen mosque building, manuscript culture and gold-based trade across the Sahel.
materials_techniques: earthen architecture; manuscript copying; gold trade; weaving; iron smithing
object_types: mosques; manuscripts; textiles; terracottas (Inland Niger Delta)
functions: exchange and value;record and writing;ritual and belief;rule and display
defined_by: Griots' oral history (Sunjata epic); Arabic sources (Ibn Battuta, al-Umari); European maps (Catalan Atlas, 1375)
leaves_out: The griot and smith (nyamakala) castes as makers and historians; non-Mande peoples; enslaved labour; Timbuktu's scholarly networks as distinct from the state; present-day Mande communities
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Gallica / BnF (public-domain items);open-access excavation reports

name: Songhay
date_note: c. 1430s to Moroccan invasion 1591
making_significance: Songhay rule at Gao and Timbuktu sustained scholarly manuscript production and Saharan trade.
materials_techniques: manuscript copying; earthen architecture; river transport
object_types: manuscripts; mosques; tomb of the Askia
functions: record and writing;exchange and value;ritual and belief;transport
defined_by: Timbuktu chronicles (Tarikh al-Sudan, Tarikh al-Fattash); French colonial scholarship
leaves_out: Earlier Songhay history at Gao; the enslaved and servile workers; Tuareg, Fulani and Bozo neighbours; present-day Songhay communities
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)

name: Kanem-Bornu
other_names: Kanem Empire; Bornu Empire; Sefuwa dynasty
date_note: c. 8th–9th century (Kanem) to 1893; Bornu phase from the late 14th century
making_significance: A long-lived Sahelian state around Lake Chad whose courts used fired-brick palaces, Arabic manuscripts, quilted cavalry armour and trans-Saharan trade goods.
materials_techniques: fired-brick building; manuscript copying; quilted cotton armour; leatherwork; horse breeding
object_types: manuscripts; brick palace ruins (e.g. Gambaru); quilted armour; horse equipment
functions: rule and display;exchange and value;war;transport;record and writing
defined_by: Arabic chronicles (e.g. Ahmad ibn Furtu, 16th c.); European travellers (Heinrich Barth, 1850s); historians
leaves_out: The Sao and other Lake Chad peoples it conquered; enslaved people traded north across the Sahara; Kanuri and neighbouring present-day communities; Buduma and Kotoko island and river peoples
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: Few free object images; mainly a search label.

name: Ife
date_note: c. 11th–15th century for the classic sculpture; settlement older and city continuing
making_significance: Ife casters and potters made naturalistic heads in copper alloy and terracotta and produced glass beads locally.
materials_techniques: lost-wax casting (copper, brass); terracotta; glass bead making; stone carving
object_types: heads; figures; glass beads; potsherd pavements
functions: ritual and belief;rule and display;clothing and adornment
defined_by: Leo Frobenius (1910), who attributed the works to outsiders; later Nigerian and British archaeology; museums
leaves_out: Frobenius's 'Atlantis' attribution; the Yoruba living tradition and the Ooni of Ife; glass-bead workers; other Yoruba centres
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;British Museum collection online (link out);open-access excavation reports

name: Benin
date_note: c. 12th century to present (kingdom conquered 1897; Oba restored 1914)
making_significance: Royal guilds (e.g. Igun Eronmwon casters) produced cast plaques, heads and ivory carving recording court history.
materials_techniques: lost-wax brass casting; ivory carving; wood carving; coral beadwork
object_types: plaques; commemorative heads; carved tusks; regalia
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing
defined_by: The Edo court; European traders and the 1897 British punitive expedition; museums worldwide
leaves_out: Not the Republic of Benin; the 1897 looting and killing; the named guilds as makers; the living court and Edo people; debates over restitution
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;British Museum collection online (link out);open-access excavation reports
notes: Restitution in progress; use only restitution-cleared or community-published images; Digital Benin (link out).

name: Kongo
date_note: c. 1390 to formal end 1914
making_significance: Kongo makers produced raffia textiles, ivory and Christian-Kongo metalwork, and power figures (minkisi).
materials_techniques: raffia weaving; brass casting; wood carving; ivory carving
object_types: raffia cloth; crucifixes; minkisi; ivory horns
functions: ritual and belief;rule and display;clothing and adornment;exchange and value
defined_by: Portuguese sources from 1483; Kongo elites' own letters; historians
leaves_out: The Atlantic slave trade that drew people from and through Kongo; neighbouring Loango, Ngoyo and Kakongo; minkisi as sacred objects; the present-day Bakongo
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;Smithsonian Open Access (CC0)

name: Mapungubwe
date_note: c. 1075–1220 CE (with K2 before)
making_significance: Mapungubwe's elite used gold foil, glass beads and ivory, an early sign of class-based settlement in southern Africa.
materials_techniques: gold foil; glass beads (imported and reworked); ivory; iron
functions: rule and display;exchange and value;ritual and belief
defined_by: University of Pretoria excavations (1933 on); South African state; UNESCO (2003)
leaves_out: Burials excavated without consent; the later Great Zimbabwe; Venda, Sotho and Shona descendant communities; apartheid-era suppression of the site's story
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)
notes: Human remains reburied 2007. Funerary material default-excluded. Routes to ARC Mapungubwe.

name: Carthaginian / Punic
date_note: traditional foundation 814 BCE to Roman destruction 146 BCE
making_significance: Carthaginian workshops made glass, masks, ivory and purple dye across the western Mediterranean.
materials_techniques: glass (core-formed); murex dye; terracotta; metal; shipbuilding
functions: exchange and value;ritual and belief;transport
defined_by: Greek and Roman writers (often hostile); French colonial archaeology; Tunisian heritage
leaves_out: Imazighen (Berbers) of the hinterland; the enslaved and mercenaries; Roman propaganda about child sacrifice (debated); later Roman Carthage
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;British Museum collection online (link out)
notes: Sub-label of CIV Phoenician; tophet material is funerary.

name: Garamantian
date_note: c. 500 BCE–700 CE
making_significance: The Garamantes built underground irrigation channels (foggaras) and towns in the Fezzan and traded across the Sahara.
materials_techniques: foggara irrigation; mud-brick building; glass and textile trade
functions: food and storage;exchange and value;shelter
defined_by: Herodotus; Roman writers; David Mattingly's Fezzan Project
leaves_out: Enslaved labour possibly used for irrigation; neighbouring Saharan pastoralists; present-day Libyan communities
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports

name: Ethiopian (Abyssinian)
date_note: Solomonic dynasty 1270–1974; label also stretched back to Aksum
making_significance: Ethiopian scriptoria produced illuminated Ge'ez manuscripts and icons, and rock-hewn churches (Lalibela).
materials_techniques: parchment manuscripts; painting; rock-cut architecture; metal processional crosses
functions: ritual and belief;record and writing;rule and display
defined_by: European travellers and orientalists; Ethiopian imperial ideology
leaves_out: Oromo, Somali, Afar and other peoples incorporated by conquest; Beta Israel and Muslim communities; the Zagwe; the looting of Maqdala (1868)
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Walters Art Museum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;British Museum collection online (link out)
notes: 'Abyssinian' is an exonym; many manuscripts from Maqdala 1868; restitution claims live.

name: Maya
date_note: c. 1000 BCE (Preclassic) to 1697 (fall of Nojpetén); Maya peoples continue today
making_significance: Maya scribes, painters, sculptors and potters produced a fully readable script, painted ceramics, stucco and carved monuments.
materials_techniques: limestone carving; stucco; polychrome ceramics; jade working; bark-paper codices; weaving
object_types: stelae; painted vessels; codices; jade; huipil textiles
functions: record and writing;rule and display;ritual and belief;clothing and adornment
defined_by: Spanish colonial writers; 19th-century explorers (Stephens and Catherwood); Mayanists; Maya communities today
leaves_out: Over 30 living Maya-language communities; the 'collapse' narrative that erases continuity; non-elite farmers; codices burned by Spanish clergy (1562); looted grave goods
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Art Institute of Chicago (CC0);Yale University Art Gallery (public-domain images);LACMA (public-domain images);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Existing in project.

name: Olmec
date_note: c. 1600–400 BCE (San Lorenzo, La Venta)
making_significance: Olmec workshops carved colossal basalt heads and small jade and greenstone figures that circulated widely.
materials_techniques: basalt carving; jade working; ceramic
object_types: colossal heads; altars; jade celts and masks; figurines
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief
defined_by: Named from the Nahuatl 'rubber people' by 20th-century archaeologists; called a 'mother culture' (contested)
leaves_out: The self-name is unknown; contemporaneous Gulf and Pacific-coast peoples framed as 'derivative'; the mother-vs-sister culture debate
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Yale University Art Gallery (public-domain images);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Routes to ARC Olmec and HOR Olmec horizon.

name: Aztec / Mexica
date_note: Tenochtitlan founded c. 1325; Spanish conquest 1521
making_significance: Mexica specialist crafts (featherwork, goldwork, stone sculpture) were organised by guilds and tribute.
materials_techniques: featherwork; lost-wax gold casting; stone sculpture; codex painting; chinampa agriculture
object_types: feather shields and headdresses; codices; stone sculpture; mosaic masks
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing;exchange and value;war
defined_by: 'Aztec' popularised by 19th-century writers (Clavijero, Humboldt, Prescott); Mexican national history
leaves_out: Tlaxcaltecs and other allies and enemies; the Triple Alliance partners Texcoco and Tlacopan; tribute-paying peoples; Nahua people today
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;Library of Congress (public-domain items)

name: Andean
date_note: c. 3000 BCE (Caral) to 1532 (Spanish invasion)
making_significance: Andean makers developed record-keeping in cords (khipu), fine textiles, metallurgy and earthwork across 5,000 years.

functions: record and writing;clothing and adornment;rule and display;food and storage;exchange and value
defined_by: Archaeologists (Julio C. Tello, Max Uhle); Peruvian national history; museums
leaves_out: Amazonian neighbours; coastal fisherfolk; Quechua and Aymara communities today; the Spanish-colonial and republican continuations
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Art Institute of Chicago (CC0);Yale University Art Gallery (public-domain images);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Existing in project. Members: CIV Caral, Chavín, Moche, Nazca, Tiwanaku, Wari, Chimú, Inca; HOR Early/Middle/Late Horizon.

name: Inca
date_note: c. 1438 (conventional) to 1572
making_significance: The Inca state organised tapestry weaving, fitted-stone architecture, road-building and khipu accounting.

name: Mississippian

functions: ritual and belief;rule and display;record and writing;exchange and value
defined_by: Arthur Evans (1900s), after the mythical King Minos
leaves_out: The self-name is unknown (Linear A undeciphered); Evans's heavy reconstructions at Knossos; non-palatial villages; forgeries of 'Minoan' goddesses
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Walters Art Museum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: Good case for F1.28a (reconstruction) and F1.14 (forgery).

name: Mycenaean
making_significance: Mycenaean palaces kept Linear B records of textile, perfume and bronze production by named workers.
materials_techniques: Linear B; gold repoussé; bronze; fresco; textile
object_types: gold masks; tablets; weapons; stirrup jars
functions: record and writing;rule and display;war;ritual and belief
defined_by: Heinrich Schliemann (1876), after Mycenae
leaves_out: Workers listed in the tablets (many women textile workers, some probably unfree); neighbours in Anatolia and the Levant; the shaft graves as burials
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports

name: Cycladic
date_note: Early Cycladic c. 3200–2000 BCE; later Cycladic to c. 1100 BCE
making_significance: Cycladic islanders carved marble figurines and vessels, many later modified to fit modernist taste.
materials_techniques: marble carving; emery abrasion; painting (lost)
functions: ritual and belief
defined_by: Archaeologists; the 20th-century art market
leaves_out: Looting for collectors (most figures unprovenanced); lost paint; forgeries
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Most figures without context; good F1.24 case.

name: Etruscan
date_note: c. 900 BCE (Villanovan) to 1st century BCE (absorbed by Rome)
making_significance: Etruscan workshops produced bronze mirrors and statues, gold granulation, bucchero and painted tombs.
materials_techniques: bronze casting and engraving; granulation; bucchero; tomb painting
functions: ritual and belief;clothing and adornment;rule and display
defined_by: Roman writers; Renaissance and 18th-century 'Etruscheria'
leaves_out: Most evidence comes from tombs; looting (tombaroli); the Villanovan roots; Italic neighbours
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Walters Art Museum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Byzantine
date_note: 330 (Constantinople) to 1453
making_significance: Byzantine workshops made mosaics, icons, silk, enamel and ivory for church and court.
materials_techniques: mosaic; icon painting; cloisonné enamel; silk weaving; ivory carving
functions: ritual and belief;rule and display;clothing and adornment
defined_by: Hieronymus Wolf (1557) coined 'Byzantine'; Enlightenment writers (Gibbon)
leaves_out: They called themselves Romans; Armenian, Slavic, Syriac and Coptic makers; enslaved people; the 1204 looting
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Walters Art Museum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Celtic
date_note: label stretched from Hallstatt (c. 800 BCE) through La Tène to early medieval Ireland and Britain
making_significance: Iron Age and early medieval metalworkers made curvilinear La Tène ornament on weapons, torcs and mirrors, later echoed in Insular manuscripts.
materials_techniques: bronze and gold smithing; enamel; repoussé; manuscript illumination
functions: clothing and adornment;war;rule and display;ritual and belief
defined_by: Greek and Roman writers ('Keltoi', 'Galli'); 18th-century antiquarians (Edward Lhuyd's language work); 19th-century nationalism and the Celtic Revival
leaves_out: The many unrelated peoples it lumps together; that ancient 'Celts' in Britain and Ireland are not so named in ancient sources; Iberian Celtiberians; the gap between language, art style and people; Romantic and nationalist inventions
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Portable Antiquities Scheme (CC BY);British Museum collection online (link out);Wikimedia Commons;Europeana (filter by rights)
notes: Routes to ARC Hallstatt and La Tène.

name: Norse / Viking
date_note: Viking Age conventionally 793–1066; Norse Greenland to c. 1450
making_significance: Norse shipwrights, smiths and carvers made clinker-built ships, pattern-welded swords, and carved wood and runestones.
materials_techniques: clinker shipbuilding; pattern welding; wood carving; textile weaving; runic inscription
functions: transport;war;clothing and adornment;record and writing;ritual and belief
defined_by: Medieval chroniclers ('vikingr' = raider); 19th-century Scandinavian nationalism; popular media
leaves_out: The enslaved people (thralls) captured and traded; Sámi neighbours and trading partners; the farmers and women weavers who made the sails; Rus' and Islamic-world partners; far-right appropriation of Norse symbols
free_sources: Swedish History Museum (CC BY);National Museum of Denmark (CC BY-SA);DM;Portable Antiquities Scheme (CC BY);Wikimedia Commons;Europeana (filter by rights)

name: Thracian
date_note: c. 1st millennium BCE to Roman annexation 46 CE
making_significance: Thracian goldsmiths made gold and silver vessels and regalia, found mostly in tumulus burials.
materials_techniques: gold and silver repoussé; tomb building; horse gear
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;clothing and adornment
defined_by: Greek writers; Bulgarian national archaeology
leaves_out: Thracians were many tribes, not one; most finds come from burials; looting of tumuli in Bulgaria
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;Europeana (filter by rights)

name: Nuragic
date_note: c. 1800 BCE to Roman conquest 238 BCE
making_significance: Sardinian communities built stone towers (nuraghi) and cast bronze figurines (bronzetti).
materials_techniques: dry-stone tower building; bronze casting
functions: shelter;ritual and belief;war
defined_by: Sardinian and Italian archaeology (Giovanni Lilliu); UNESCO (Su Nuraxi, 1997)
leaves_out: The label implies a unified state; Phoenician and Punic neighbours; present-day Sardinians
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Europeana (filter by rights);UNESCO World Heritage listing (link out)

name: Old Europe
date_note: c. 6500–3500 BCE (Neolithic and Copper Age southeastern Europe)
making_significance: A label for Neolithic Balkan and Carpathian farming societies known for figurines, painted pottery and early copper and gold.
materials_techniques: painted pottery; clay figurines; copper and gold working
functions: ritual and belief;food and storage;clothing and adornment
defined_by: Marija Gimbutas (1970s), with a contested 'goddess' interpretation
leaves_out: The diversity of cultures (Vinča, Cucuteni–Trypillia, Varna, Karanovo); the contested gender narrative; later populations
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Europeana (filter by rights)
notes: Routes to ARC Vinča (existing), Cucuteni–Trypillia, Varna.

name: Moorish
date_note: 711 to the final expulsions of Moriscos 1609–1614
making_significance: The label covers Andalusi and Maghribi workshops that made lustreware, carved ivory, silks, stucco and tilework.
materials_techniques: lustreware; ivory carving; silk weaving; stucco; zellij tilework
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;clothing and adornment
defined_by: Medieval Christian chroniclers ('Mauri'); Romantic travellers; Spanish and Moroccan heritage
leaves_out: It flattens Arabs, Imazighen, Muslims, converts, Jews and Mozarabs into one term with racialised overtones; Mudéjar and Morisco makers under Christian rule; the expelled
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Routes to CIV Islamic; label to explain, not endorse.

name: Western
date_note: a modern label claiming a line from Greece and Rome to modern Europe and North America
making_significance: A curriculum label that organised much of museum and design-history teaching around European making.
defined_by: 19th–20th-century European and US universities ('Western Civ' courses, from c. 1919 in the US); Samuel Huntington (1996)
leaves_out: Everything outside Europe and its settler colonies; the Islamic, Byzantine and African roots it borrows from; the colonised and enslaved whose labour and objects built its museums
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons
notes: Search label; card explains the label.

name: Islamic
date_note: 622 (hijra) to present
making_significance: A label for the makers of many societies whose shared features include Arabic script, calligraphy, geometric ornament, glazed ceramics, carpets and metalwork.
materials_techniques: calligraphy; lustreware; inlaid metal; carpet knotting; paper
functions: record and writing;ritual and belief;rule and display;clothing and adornment;exchange and value
defined_by: European art history and museums ('Islamic art' departments, 19th c.)
leaves_out: Non-Muslim makers (Christians, Jews, Zoroastrians) within Islamic societies; enslaved workers; regional traditions (West African, Southeast Asian, Chinese Muslim) often left out; present-day Muslim communities
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Walters Art Museum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Existing in project.

name: Scythian
date_note: c. 9th–3rd century BCE
making_significance: Scythian and related steppe peoples made gold 'animal style' ornaments, horse gear and felt, preserved mainly in kurgan burials.
materials_techniques: gold casting and repoussé; felt making; horse equipment
object_types: plaques; pectorals; bridle ornaments; felt hangings
functions: clothing and adornment;rule and display;transport;war
defined_by: Herodotus; Russian imperial collecting (Peter I's Siberian collection); Soviet archaeology
leaves_out: The many different peoples grouped under one name; most finds come from graves; Greek goldsmiths who made some pieces; looting
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Sogdian
date_note: c. 6th century BCE to c. 10th century CE
making_significance: Sogdian merchants and makers produced silver vessels, wall paintings and silks and carried goods across the Silk Road.
materials_techniques: silverwork; wall painting; silk weaving
functions: exchange and value;rule and display;ritual and belief
defined_by: Greek and Persian sources; Chinese records; 20th-century archaeology (Panjikent, Afrasiab)
leaves_out: Sogdian diaspora communities in China, whose funerary couches mix traditions; the plural identities of merchants; enslaved people traded on the same routes; the Arab conquest and later Islamic Sogdiana
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Oxus
making_significance: Oxus (BMAC) settlements made compartmented seals and composite stone 'princess' figures.
materials_techniques: soft-stone carving; metal casting
functions: ritual and belief;rule and display
defined_by: Viktor Sarianidi (1970s); French archaeology (Henri-Paul Francfort)
leaves_out: The large number of looted and faked 'Bactrian' objects on the market; neighbouring Andronovo and Namazga communities; present-day Turkmen, Uzbek and Afghan communities
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Routes to ARC Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex.

name: Polynesian
date_note: Lapita arrival c. 900 BCE (Tonga, Samoa) to present
making_significance: Polynesian makers built voyaging canoes, barkcloth, carved wood and stone, and navigation without instruments.
materials_techniques: canoe building; barkcloth (tapa); wood and stone carving; featherwork
functions: transport;clothing and adornment;ritual and belief;rule and display
defined_by: Jules Dumont d'Urville (1831); European voyagers
leaves_out: Living Polynesian nations (Māori, Hawaiian, Samoan, Tongan, Tahitian and others) and their own names and histories; the European racial ranking that set Polynesia above Melanesia; Micronesian and Melanesian neighbours; taonga taken to museums
free_sources: Te Papa Collections Online (CC BY where marked);Auckland Museum Collections Online (CC BY);Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Lapita
date_note: c. 1350–500 BCE from the Bismarck Archipelago to Tonga and Samoa
making_significance: Lapita potters stamped intricate dentate designs on pottery as their communities voyaged into Remote Oceania for the first time.
materials_techniques: dentate-stamped pottery; obsidian exchange; shell ornament; canoe voyaging
object_types: dentate-stamped pots; shell rings; obsidian tools
functions: food and storage;ritual and belief;transport;exchange and value
defined_by: Archaeologists, after the Lapita site in New Caledonia (excavated 1952)
leaves_out: Not a civilisation or state; the earlier Papuan-speaking peoples of Near Oceania; descendant Pacific communities who hold the designs in tattoo and tapa
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;Auckland Museum Collections Online (CC BY)
notes: FLAG: rarely called a civilisation; label kept because searched. Routes to ARC Lapita (existing) and HOR Lapita horizon.

name: Rapa Nui
date_note: settlement c. 1150–1250 CE to present
making_significance: Rapa Nui carvers quarried and moved nearly a thousand moai and made rongorongo tablets and wood carvings.
materials_techniques: volcanic tuff carving; wood carving; rongorongo incision
functions: ritual and belief;record and writing;rule and display
defined_by: European voyagers (Roggeveen, 1722); Jared Diamond's 'collapse' account (2005) and its critics
leaves_out: The 'ecocide' myth, contested by evidence that slave raids (1862) and introduced disease caused the population crash; the living Rapa Nui people; moai held abroad (e.g. Hoa Hakananai'a) and return requests
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: Good F1.3 case: no 'rise and fall' unless evidence supports it.

name: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
date_note: occupation of Australia from at least c. 65,000–50,000 years ago (debated) to present
making_significance: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander makers have developed rock art, ground-edge axes, fibre work, eel-trap aquaculture and painting over tens of thousands of years.
materials_techniques: rock painting and engraving; ground-edge stone; fibre weaving; bark painting; aquaculture
object_types: rock art; stone tools; fibre bags; bark paintings; shields
functions: ritual and belief;tools;food and storage;clothing and adornment;record and writing
defined_by: Popular media and government campaigns ('oldest continuous culture'); Aboriginal organisations
leaves_out: More than 250 language groups with their own names and laws; Torres Strait Islanders as distinct; that the phrase can freeze living cultures in the past; stolen objects and remains held in museums
free_sources: Museums Victoria Collections (CC BY / public domain);Wikimedia Commons;community-published site
notes: Date: Madjedbebe claim c. 65,000 BP is debated; 'civilisation' is not a self-description; community consultation required.
